extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, intellectuals, and policymakers interested in culture, religion, and national life (Victorian public/intellectual audience)
extracted.subtask_description: An essay setting out standards for what 'culture' should be — its aims, methods, and institutional implications — and critiquing religious, political, and educational arrangements that hinder or promote cultural totality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality (harmonious perfection of the whole being)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture aims at the harmonious perfection of our whole being — what we call totality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions and education should cultivate many sides of a person so as to produce 'totality' rather than a narrow, one-sided development. Anti-patterns include universities or systems that train only technical skills (miners, engineers) and fail to produce 'sweetness and light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture enjoins disinterestedness — obedience not to likings or party-partisanship but to the aim of human perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural judgement should be independent of partisan sympathies or fashionable aims; avoid using 'culture' as a cloak for factional interests. Example: one should not take a Church's part from political expediency; anti-patterns include Benthamism or treating cultural ends like party platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and independence of machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is independent of particular machinery (institutions); the same inward perfection can be reached with different external forms (free churches or established churches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose institutional means pragmatically and change them when they cease to serve the end; do not treat a specific institutional form as itself an absolute. Anti-pattern: rigid attachment to forms or systems as ends in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact with the main current of national/human life
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture requires being in contact with the main current of national and human life; this contact is more important for spiritual growth than holding a particular speculative opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions (e.g., national churches, universities) should bring individuals into wider cultural and historical sympathy rather than isolating them. Anti-pattern: 'hole-and-corner' churches or voluntaryism that keeps people out of the main stream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid provincialism / oppose Hebraising as totalising narrowness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebraising (an overvalued, narrow religious/doing emphasis) produces provincialism by making one spiritual side swallow others and so thwarts culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of formations that excite only a single spiritual faculty (religious earnestness in a narrow way) at the cost of other gifts (Hellenic knowing, aesthetic and intellectual cultivation). Example: the essay argues America 'Hebraises' and thus lacks full culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect religious earnestness without sacrificing totality
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture recognises and pays tribute to the religious side in man (its worth and divine quality) but refuses to surrender man's totality to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value prayer-books, liturgy and sincere devotion while ensuring they remain parts of a broader cultural life. Anti-pattern: treating religion as the only legitimate spiritual cultivation or reducing all culture to sectarian orthodoxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Hellenism and Hebraism
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture needs both Hellenising (knowledge, intellectual cultivation) and Hebraising (devout energy and moral doing); praise Hellenism when Hebraism has been excessive, but be ready to restore Hebraism's virtues later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not permanently privilege one tendency; recognise each has moments of preeminence. Anti-pattern: permanent swing to either pure intellectualism or pure devout activism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose Mialism (doctrine that isolates groups / 'holes and corners')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt doctrines that leave groups in isolation ('holes and corners') or divorce sections of the nation from the main current of life as a way of granting equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies meant to placate separatists by detaching everyone (cutting off 'tails all round') are mistaken unless it can be shown that attachment to the mainstream has no value. Anti-pattern: universal voluntaryism that produces cultural fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keen sense of what is really fatal (prioritisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture has a keen sense of what is really fatal to spiritual and national life and is permissive about matters that are not fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus energy on avoiding the gravest errors (e.g., complacent self-congratulation, mistaking political machinery for inward progress) while being tolerant about lesser disagreements. Anti-pattern: treating non-fatal matters as decisive and neglecting more serious dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inward working over machinery/political activism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer inward cultivation and moral/intellectual formation to exclusive concentration on political machinery or instrumental reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cultural education and inner change rather than assuming political measures alone (free trade, franchise extension) will secure human perfection. Anti-pattern: believing that success in a set of political nostrums equals cultural progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional inclusion to remedy provincialism
rubrics_metrics.description: To cure provincialism among dissenters, recognise and regularise popular church-discipline within national institutions (e.g., establish a Congregational/Presbyterian church on equal terms with the Episcopal Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical policy recommendation: integrate important elements of dissenting practice into national structures so that separation ceases to be the rule. Anti-pattern: violent exclusion or simply denouncing dissent without institutional remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-attachment to chosen means (willingness to move beyond machinery)
rubrics_metrics.description: After selecting machinery that serves cultural ends, culture should not 'hold stiffly and blindly' to that machinery but should move on when necessary for the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutions instrumentally, and be ready to discard or reform them for the greater aim of sweetness and light. Anti-pattern: sanctifying means and refusing to adapt once they are no longer fit for purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness and light as cultural ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture aims at 'sweetness and light'—intellectual refinement, clarity, and humane illumination of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ideal is not mere pedantry; it is a substantive goal of education and public life. Anti-pattern: dismissing culture as mere smattering of 'dead languages' or equating it with impractical pedantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions should give a sense of historical life
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions (like established churches and universities) tend to give people a sense of a historical life of the human spirit beyond their private fancies, and thereby suggest new sympathies to cultivate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recognised public culture and settled institutions provide leisure and perspective that prevent narrow invention of forms and enable broader spiritual growth. Anti-pattern: societies lacking such institutions produce one-sided spiritual life and relentless reinvention of sectarian forms.
